client: I just don't know how I'm supposed to focus on studying for finals when all I can think about is my grandpa. Every time I open a textbook, I just remember how proud he was of me going to college, and then I start crying. Part of me feels like I shouldn't even be here talking about this when I have exams coming up, but I can't seem to get my mind straight.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this deep love for your grandpa alongside the pressure of exams, and that collision feels overwhelming right now. I'm hearing how much he believed in you - might that belief be something to hold onto as you navigate this difficult time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know he believed in me, but that almost makes it harder. What if I let him down by not doing well? The pressure feels even heavier now that he's gone. Sometimes I think he'd be disappointed if he saw how anxious I've become about these tests.
therapist: Your voice carries so much care and concern about honoring his memory, and I wonder if that pressure might be clouding how you see yourself through his eyes. What do you think he would say about needing to be perfect versus simply doing your best?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client:
You know, I never really thought about it that way. He was always so encouraging when I was growing up, always telling me that effort mattered more than perfection. But now that he's gone, I feel like I have to be perfect to make him proud, like anything less would disappoint him somehow. It's like this pressure just keeps building, and I don't know how to let it go. 

Sometimes I wonder if I'm just imagining what he'd want, or if I'm putting these expectations on myself more than he ever would have. But even knowing that doesn't make the feeling go away.
therapist: I hear both the warmth when you recall his encouraging words and this painful gap between what you believe he truly valued and what you're demanding of yourself now. Could we explore what it might feel like to give yourself the same kindness he so clearly gave you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: It’s hard to imagine being kind to myself in the way he was. He saw the best in me, but I feel like I’ve let him down since he’s been gone. I keep thinking about all the things I should’ve done differently, and it’s like I don’t deserve that same kindness now. It feels easier to hold onto the guilt than to try to let it go.
therapist: The way your voice softens when you speak about his belief in you shows how deeply you carry his love, even as your words wrestle with feeling undeserving. What would it be like, just for a moment, to imagine speaking to yourself with the same gentle patience he showed you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: It’s hard for me to imagine speaking to myself that way because I feel like I don’t deserve it. I keep thinking about all the mistakes I’ve made and how I’ve let people down—it’s like his kindness was for a version of me that doesn’t really exist anymore. Trying to be gentle with myself feels fake, like I’m pretending to be someone I’m not.
therapist: I hear how painful it feels to reach for that kindness, like you're reaching for something that belonged to a different version of yourself. That sense of disconnect—between who you were then and who you are now—sounds like it's carrying a lot of weight. What comes up for you when you consider that perhaps the "you" he believed in is still here, just struggling under all these layers of guilt?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: I want to believe that version of me still exists somewhere, but it just feels buried too deep. The guilt is so heavy—like every mistake I've made has piled up and crushed that person. Sometimes I think maybe he was wrong about me all along, and now I'm just proving him right by failing.
therapist: Your voice trembles with such raw pain when you talk about feeling crushed by guilt—it sounds like you're carrying this immense burden of proving yourself worthy of his belief. That image of his faith in you being buried under all these mistakes—might we gently explore what it would take to start clearing some of that weight away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know if I can clear any of this weight away. Every time I try to move forward, I just remember all the disappointed looks and broken promises. It's like his belief in me was this precious gift, and I smashed it to pieces without even realizing what I was doing.
therapist: The way you describe that precious gift of his belief—your voice slows and drops when you talk about it—shows just how much it meant to you. I wonder if that gift might still be whole, even if it feels shattered right now—what would it be like to consider that his belief in you wasn’t something you could break, even when you stumble?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
That's a really beautiful way to look at it... but I don't know if I can believe that. When I mess up, it feels like I'm proving him wrong, like I never deserved that belief in the first place. The harder I try to live up to it, the more I feel like I'm failing. 

It's just... if his belief was really unbreakable, why do I feel so crushed under the weight of it? Like I'm constantly disappointing someone who's not even here anymore.
therapist: I hear the struggle in your voice—this tension between wanting to honor his belief in you and feeling like you're constantly falling short. That word "crushed" stands out—what would it feel like to imagine that his belief wasn't a weight to carry, but something more like a hand on your shoulder, steadying you even when you stumble?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of seeing it as a steadying hand instead of a weight, but honestly it still feels heavy to me. When I think about him believing in me, all I can focus on is how I might disappoint him—like his faith in me is this fragile thing I could break at any moment. It's hard to shift that perspective when the fear feels so real.
therapist: It sounds like that fear of disappointing him is holding onto you tightly, even as you try to see his belief differently. What would it feel like to imagine him sitting beside you right now—what might he say about carrying this fear of breaking his faith in you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... the idea of him sitting here actually makes me more anxious. He'd probably say something supportive, but I can't shake this feeling that he's just being nice and secretly disappointed in me. That's the worst part - when people are kind but I think they're just hiding their true feelings. 

Even trying to imagine this conversation makes my chest feel tight. What if I'm right and he actually does feel let down? I've seen that look before from other people when they think I've failed them.
therapist: I notice your voice lifts when you imagine his kindness, even as your words carry this deep worry that it might not be genuine—that tension between hope and fear sounds so painful. When you mention seeing that "look" from others, I wonder if those past experiences might be coloring how you imagine he would see you now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
